title: Conduct routine maintenance of technical- and site equipment

lessons.title: What routine maintenance is and why it matters
lessons.html:
What routine maintenance is

Routine maintenance is the small, regular care that keeps equipment working: cleaning, checking, greasing, tightening and reporting. It is done every day, every week or every month, by a schedule. It is not the big repairs that a fitter or electrician does.

At a silo, equipment includes conveyors, belts, elevators, slides, augers, fans, the weighbridge, sample tools, scales, hand trucks, the bakkie or tractor, and site items such as gates, fences, lights and drains.

Why it matters

  • A machine that is looked after breaks less. Breakdowns in harvest time leave trucks waiting and farmers angry.
  • Small problems found early are cheap to fix. A worn bearing costs little. A burnt-out motor costs thousands of rand.
  • Well-kept machines are safer. Loose guards, worn belts and leaking oil cause injuries and fires.
  • Clean equipment keeps grain clean.

The maintenance schedule

Your site has a schedule or checklist. It tells you:

  • Which equipment to check.
  • What to check: for example belt tension, oil level, grease points, noise, heat.
  • How often: daily, weekly, monthly.
  • Who does it.
  • Where to sign.
EquipmentDaily check example
ConveyorGuards in place, belt running straight, no spilt grain
BakkieOil, water, tyres, lights
WeighbridgeDeck clean, no stones under the edges
Scale in the labClean and reads zero

Only do the tasks you are trained and allowed to do. Electrical work is done only by qualified electricians.

Write down what you did and anything strange you saw. These records show when parts were last greased or changed, and help the fitter find the cause of a breakdown.

lessons.title: Doing maintenance safely and reporting faults
lessons.html:
Doing maintenance safely

Lock out first

Most injuries during maintenance happen because a machine starts while someone is working on it. Before you clean, grease or tighten anything on a machine:

  1. Tell the control room and your supervisor.
  2. Switch the machine off at the isolator.
  3. Put your own lock and tag on the isolator. Only you have the key.
  4. Try to start the machine to make sure it is dead. Then switch back to off.
  5. Wait for all parts to stop moving.
  6. When finished, put the guards back, remove your tools, check everyone is clear, then remove your lock.

Never work on a machine that someone else locked out without speaking to them. Never remove another person's lock.

Common routine tasks

  • Cleaning: remove dust, grain and spilt oil. Dust on motors makes them overheat.
  • Greasing: grease each nipple on the schedule with the right grease. Wipe the nipple first. Do not over-grease.
  • Checking oil: check levels in gearboxes and engines and top up with the right oil.
  • Tightening: loose bolts on guards and covers.
  • Looking and listening: new noises, smells, heat, vibration or leaks.

Reporting faults

  • If you find a fault you cannot fix, report it straight away on the fault report or job card.
  • Say what equipment, where, what you saw, and when.
  • If the fault is dangerous, tag the machine do not use and tell your supervisor.

Care for the environment

Catch old oil in a drip tray. Put used oil and greasy rags in the marked containers. Never pour oil into drains or onto the ground.

Key points

  • Routine maintenance is regular cleaning, checking, greasing and reporting.
  • Follow the maintenance schedule and sign it.
  • Always switch off and lock out before working on a machine.
  • Put guards back before you remove your lock.
  • Report faults on the job card and dispose of oil correctly.
